city.name: Buenos Aires
city.subtitle: Immigration, community and resilience
city.description: Visit major institutions and memorials of Latin America's largest Jewish community.

tour.title: Jewish Buenos Aires: Immigration, Community and Resilience
tour.subtitle: Worship, archives, Holocaust memory and public remembrance
tour.overview: This urban route connects the historic Templo Libertad and Jewish Museum with AMIA, the Holocaust Museum and the memorial plaza at the former Israeli Embassy.

stops.title: Templo Libertad
stops.shortDescription: Argentina's first purpose-built synagogue and the historic home of the Congregación Israelita de la República Argentina.
stops.fullDescription: The synagogue developed in stages from the late nineteenth century and was inaugurated in its enlarged form in 1932. Its Romanesque-influenced façade and civic location express the growing presence of Argentine Jewry. It remains an active congregation with controlled access.
stops.transcript: Templo Libertad stands near some of Argentina's leading civic and cultural institutions, a position that reflects the Jewish community's growing confidence in Buenos Aires. The Congregación Israelita de la República Argentina traces its organised history to the nineteenth century, and this site became the country's first purpose-built synagogue. The present monumental form was inaugurated in 1932 after enlargement of an earlier building. Its façade, organ, galleries and sanctuary express a European-influenced liturgical tradition adapted to Argentine public life. Jewish migration to Argentina included people from Central and Eastern Europe, the Ottoman world, North Africa and elsewhere, producing communities with different languages and customs. This synagogue represents an important national institution, but not the whole of that diversity. It remains a place of worship and may require advance booking, identification and security screening. Begin here by considering how architecture communicates both religious continuity and a claim to equal citizenship in the city.

stops.title: Dr. Salvador Kibrick Jewish Museum
stops.shortDescription: A museum within the Templo Libertad complex documenting Jewish worship, immigration and participation in Argentine society.
stops.fullDescription: The museum preserves ritual objects, manuscripts, historical documents and artworks related to Jews in Argentina. Its location beside the synagogue links public history with a living congregation. Access normally follows the institution's current booking and security arrangements.
stops.transcript: The Dr. Salvador Kibrick Jewish Museum expands the story from one synagogue to Jewish life across Argentina. Its collections include ceremonial objects, immigration records, manuscripts, art and documents showing how communities built schools, charities, congregations and cultural organisations. A Torah ornament or family photograph can connect religious practice with the practical experience of migration. Argentina offered opportunity and at times refuge, yet Jewish residents also faced antisemitism and political upheaval. The museum helps visitors hold these realities together rather than presenting a simple success story. It is named for a historian and communal figure who worked to preserve this record. Because the museum shares the secure Templo Libertad complex, entry and opening hours must be confirmed rather than assumed. This stop intentionally shares a location with the synagogue, but asks a different question: how does a community select objects to explain itself to future generations and to the wider country? Look for individual names and places of origin behind broad labels such as immigrant or Argentine Jew.

stops.title: AMIA and Pasteur Memorial
stops.shortDescription: The rebuilt centre of Argentina's Jewish mutual association and a site of remembrance for the 1994 bombing victims.
stops.fullDescription: AMIA is a central Jewish social and mutual-aid institution. On 18 July 1994 a bombing destroyed its headquarters and killed 85 people. The rebuilt secure building, nearby art and Pasteur–AMIA station memorials sustain public memory while AMIA continues communal work. The interior is not a casual visitor site.
stops.transcript: AMIA began as a mutual-aid organisation serving Jewish immigrants and grew into a major centre for welfare, employment, culture, education and burial services. On 18 July 1994, a terrorist bombing destroyed the building at Pasteur 633, killing eighty-five people and injuring hundreds. The attack remains the deadliest terrorist atrocity in Argentina. The headquarters was rebuilt with substantial security, making continued communal work itself a statement of resilience. Memorials in the area and artistic interventions in the nearby Pasteur–AMIA underground station repeat names, faces and demands for justice. Do not photograph security arrangements or expect public access to the building. Stand at an appropriate distance and focus on the victims as individuals rather than on the spectacle of violence. The unresolved and contested history of the investigation is part of Argentina's public debate, but this tour's first responsibility is remembrance and recognition of AMIA as a living institution whose purpose extends far beyond the attack.

stops.title: Buenos Aires Holocaust Museum
stops.shortDescription: Argentina's principal museum for Holocaust education, survivor testimony and the history of refugees who rebuilt lives in the country.
stops.fullDescription: The museum presents the Holocaust through artefacts, documents and testimony, with particular attention to survivors and refugees in Argentina. It also examines Nazi ideology, persecution and local responses. Visitors should allow time for emotionally demanding material and check admission requirements.
stops.transcript: The Buenos Aires Holocaust Museum places European destruction within an Argentine setting. Survivors who came to the country carried languages, professions, family memories and the absence of relatives who had been murdered. Their testimony became central to education here. Exhibitions explain the rise of Nazism, exclusion, ghettos, deportation and mass murder while using personal objects and voices to resist reducing six million Jewish victims to a number. The museum also invites questions about Argentina: refugee policies, post-war migration, public memory and the presence of both survivors and Nazi fugitives. These subjects require evidence and care, not myths or sensational claims. Give yourself time, especially when listening to testimony. The museum is an educational institution with scheduled hours and security procedures. Its place in this route connects immigrant community life to a catastrophe that transformed Argentine Jewry, as survivors rebuilt families and organisations while insisting that the experiences they carried should enter national memory.

stops.title: Israeli Embassy Memorial Plaza
stops.address: Arroyo and Suipacha, Buenos Aires, Argentina
stops.shortDescription: A public memorial on the site of the Israeli Embassy destroyed by a terrorist bombing in 1992.
stops.fullDescription: The 17 March 1992 bombing destroyed the embassy and killed 22 identified victims while injuring hundreds. The memorial plaza preserves the outline of the lost building and uses rows of linden trees to remember those killed. It is a public place of civic and diplomatic remembrance.
stops.transcript: This quiet plaza occupies the site where the Israeli Embassy stood until 17 March 1992. A terrorist bombing destroyed the building, killed twenty-two identified victims and injured hundreds of people in the surrounding area. The dead included embassy staff, neighbours, passers-by and people working nearby, making the attack a wound in both Jewish and Argentine civic life. The memorial preserves a trace of the former building on an adjoining wall. Two rows of linden trees represent the identified victims, replacing destroyed architecture with living markers that change through the seasons. The attack preceded the AMIA bombing by two years, and the two events remain linked in public memory and demands for justice. Walk through without treating the site as a backdrop. Read available names and inscriptions, and remember that memorial design often speaks through absence. Ending here moves the tour into shared urban space: the loss is connected to Jewish and Israeli institutions, but it belongs to the history of Buenos Aires as a whole.
